title: Extracting a coordinate axis from an additive kernel after separable extension
statement: Let $k$ be a field of prime characteristic $p>0$ [def-weil-field], let $n\geq1$, and put $E=\mathbf G_a^n$ [def-sc-gm-ga, def-sc-group-scheme]. Let $f:E\to\mathbf G_a$ be a $k$-group-scheme homomorphism, and let $K/k$ be a separable closure, meaning a separably closed algebraic separable extension. Write $\mathbb A^1_K=\operatorname{Spec}K[t]$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum, def-weil-polynomial-ring]. Suppose there is a nonconstant $K$-scheme morphism $u:\mathbb A^1_K\to E_K$ such that $f_K\circ u=0$. There is a $k$-group automorphism $\alpha:E\xrightarrow{\sim}E$ such that $f\circ\alpha$ factors through the projection $\pi:E\to\mathbf G_a^{n-1}$ onto the last $n-1$ coordinates: $f\circ\alpha=g\circ\pi$ for a $k$-group homomorphism $g:\mathbf G_a^{n-1}\to\mathbf G_a$. In particular $\alpha(\mathbf G_a\times\{0\}^{n-1})\subseteq\ker(f)$ as subgroup schemes, with the kernel the fibre over the zero section. For $n=1$ the conclusion means $f=0$. The automorphism need not be linear, and $k$ need not be perfect.

source.place: Lemma 1.11, printed pp.6--7, and Lemma 1.13, printed p.7, using Lemma 1.12 for Galois descent of a principal-part zero; the n=1 degree argument is included. Read online at https://math.stanford.edu/~conrad/papers/appbnew.pdf; WANTED locally. No Stacks tag is claimed for this algebraic-group result.

proof.text: Use the affine-spectrum dictionary [def-weil-affine-spectrum] and the polynomial universal property [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring]: $\operatorname{Spec}k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ represents the product of $n$ copies of $\mathbf G_a$, since a map into it is precisely a tuple of images of the $x_i$. Thus $f$ is a polynomial $F$ satisfying $F(X+Y)=F(X)+F(Y)$ by the comultiplication in [def-sc-gm-ga]. Its constant term is zero. Separate this identity by total degree; each nonzero homogeneous component satisfies the same additive identity. Apply [lem-trf-additive-polynomial-monomial-classification] to each positive-degree component and sum. This gives $F=\sum_i F_i(x_i)$ with $F_i(T)=\sum_j c_{ij}T^{p^j}$, and the same description holds after any $k$-group coordinate automorphism. Conversely these sums are additive over every $k$-algebra by [def-weil-ring-frobenius].

source.place: Proposition 1.6, Definition 1.10, Lemma 1.11 (1)⇒(2)⇒(3), printed pp.5–7, and Lemmas 1.12–1.13, printed p.7; read online at https://math.stanford.edu/~conrad/papers/appbnew.pdf; local copy WANTED.

proof.text: If $F=0$, choose $\alpha=\mathrm{id}$ and $g=0$. More generally, whenever some $F_i=0$, permute that coordinate to the first position and omit it to obtain $g$. Hence consider a current polynomial $Q=\sum_i Q_i(x_i)$ with every $Q_i\ne0$. Write $\deg Q_i=p^{m_i}$ and its leading coefficient as $c_i\ne0$, and call $P_Q=\sum_i c_i x_i^{p^{m_i}}$ its principal part. We will use strong induction on the positive integer $D(Q)=\sum_i\deg Q_i$, allowing the zero-coordinate case as a terminal case.

source.place: Proposition 1.6, Definition 1.10, Lemma 1.11 (1)⇒(2)⇒(3), printed pp.5–7, and Lemmas 1.12–1.13, printed p.7; read online at https://math.stanford.edu/~conrad/papers/appbnew.pdf; local copy WANTED.

proof.text: For every current $Q$ obtained by a $k$-group coordinate automorphism $\beta$, the curve $v=\beta_K^{-1}\circ u$ remains nonconstant and satisfies $Q_K(v)=0$. By [def-weil-affine-spectrum], write its coordinates as $v_i(t)\in K[t]$. Put $s_i=\deg v_i$ when nonconstant and $s_i=0$ otherwise, and let $A_i$ be the leading coefficient when $s_i>0$. Then $N=\max_i(s_i p^{m_i})>0$. The coefficient of $t^N$ in $Q_K(v)$ is $\sum_{s_i p^{m_i}=N}c_i A_i^{p^{m_i}}$: all lower terms of each $Q_i(v_i)$ have smaller degree, and constant $v_i$ contribute no positive degree. Set $a_i=A_i$ for these maximal indices and $a_i=0$ otherwise. At least one $a_i\ne0$, and $P_Q(a)=0$. Apply [lem-sfb-diagonal-p-form-separable-isotropy-descent] with $L=K$, which is algebraic separable by hypothesis, to obtain $b\in k^n\setminus\{0\}$ with $P_Q(b)=0$. This argument applies anew after every coordinate change; no descent of $u$ is asserted.

source.place: Proposition 1.6, Definition 1.10, Lemma 1.11 (1)⇒(2)⇒(3), printed pp.5–7, and Lemmas 1.12–1.13, printed p.7; read online at https://math.stanford.edu/~conrad/papers/appbnew.pdf; local copy WANTED.

proof.text: Permute the coordinates and the tuple $b$ together so $m_1\ge\cdots\ge m_n$, and let $r$ be the least index with $b_r\ne0$. Define the polynomial substitution $S$ by $x_i=y_i$ for $i<r$, $x_r=b_r y_r$, and $x_i=y_i+b_i y_r^{p^{m_r-m_i}}$ for $i>r$. It is additive by [def-weil-ring-frobenius] and has polynomial inverse $y_r=x_r/b_r$, $y_i=x_i$ for $i<r$, and $y_i=x_i-b_i(x_r/b_r)^{p^{m_r-m_i}}$ for $i>r$; hence it is a $k$-group automorphism by the affine-spectrum dictionary. In $Q\circ S$ the coefficient of $y_r^{p^{m_r}}$ is $\sum_{i\ge r}c_i b_i^{p^{m_i}}=P_Q(b)=0$. Each lower term of $Q_i$ for $i>r$, after substitution, contributes a $y_r$ power strictly below $p^{m_r}$, since $p^j p^{m_r-m_i}<p^{m_r}$ for $j<m_i$; the same strict bound holds for lower terms of $Q_r$. All coordinate polynomials in $y_i$ with $i\ne r$ retain their old degrees. Thus either the $y_r$ coordinate polynomial vanishes or $D(Q\circ S)<D(Q)$. In the latter case the curve $S_K^{-1}\circ v$ verifies the induction hypothesis for the new polynomial, by step 3. Strong induction therefore reaches a zero coordinate. This also covers degree-one terms ($m_i=0$); it extracts no $p$th root in $k$.

source.place: Proposition 1.6, Definition 1.10, Lemma 1.11 (1)⇒(2)⇒(3), printed pp.5–7, and Lemmas 1.12–1.13, printed p.7; read online at https://math.stanford.edu/~conrad/papers/appbnew.pdf; local copy WANTED.

proof.text: Compose the finitely many permutations and substitutions with the terminal permutation putting the zero coordinate first, and call the resulting automorphism $\alpha$. The polynomial for $f\circ\alpha$ is a sum involving only $x_2,\ldots,x_n$, so the same sum defines the $k$-group homomorphism $g$ with $f\circ\alpha=g\circ\pi$. These are polynomial identities, hence hold on every $k$-algebra, including algebras with nilpotents; the first factor therefore maps into the scheme-theoretic kernel (the fibre over zero in [def-sc-group-scheme]). For $n=1$, a nonzero $F$ would give $\deg(F(v_1))=(\deg F)(\deg v_1)>0$, contradicting $F(v_1)=0$. Thus $f=0$ in that case, with $g$ the zero map from $\mathbf G_a^0=\operatorname{Spec}k$.
